parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a community garden to ask about renting a plot.
script: Good morning, Riverside Community Garden, Tom speaking.
Oh, hello. I saw your poster at the station, and I'm interested in renting a plot.
Great. Let me take some details. What's your name?
Could you spell the surname for me?
Sure. K, A, P, O, O, R.
Is that M, I, L, L?
Now, we have two plot sizes. The small ones are ten square metres, and the large ones are twenty.
I was thinking of a large one, but honestly, I've never grown anything before, so I'd better start with a small one.
Very sensible. A lot of beginners take on too much. The small plots cost forty-five pounds a year, and the large ones are seventy-five.
Forty-five is fine. Does that include tools?
Yes. We have a shed full of spades, forks and watering cans that members can borrow. But you'll need to bring your own gloves. We don't provide those, for hygiene reasons.
OK. Is there some sort of introduction for new members?
Yes, everyone attends an induction session. We run them on Wednesday evenings and Saturday mornings. The Wednesday one this month is already full, I'm afraid.
Good. I'll put you down for Saturday at ten.
What about watering? Is there a tap?
There's no tap on the site. We collect rainwater from the shed roofs in large barrels, and members fill their cans from those.
That's very eco-friendly. Are there any rules I should know about?
Just a few. No bonfires, and no chemical pesticides of any kind. We're an organic garden, so we encourage natural methods, like planting marigolds to keep insects away.
I love that idea. Do you run any courses?
We do. There's a composting workshop next month. It was going to be in the garden itself, but because of the weather we've moved it to the library on Station Street.
Great, I'll look out for that. How do members find out about events?
Through our newsletter. It used to come out every month, but there's so much going on now that we send it every fortnight.
You're welcome, Priya. See you on Saturday.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A volunteer coordinator talks to new volunteers at a marine centre.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Harbour Marine Centre. My name's Hannah, and I coordinate our volunteer programme. Before we walk round, I'd like to give you some background and explain how your first week will work.

The centre opened in 1998 as a small aquarium run by the local fishing community. In those days, the main aim was to show tourists what lived in the bay. Over time, though, our focus has shifted. Today, our most important work is rescuing and treating injured sea animals, especially seals and turtles, and returning them to the wild. Education is still part of what we do, but it's no longer the main purpose.

Many of you have asked how many volunteers we have. In summer, the number can reach about a hundred and twenty, but at this time of year it's closer to forty, which is why we're so pleased to see you here.

Now, your first week. On Monday, you'll shadow an experienced volunteer. You won't handle any animals at all during your first week. I know some of you are keen, but safety comes first. What we'd most like you to concentrate on is learning the daily routines, particularly the cleaning and feeding schedules.
As for uniform, we'll give you two T-shirts and a fleece. The one thing you must provide yourself is a pair of waterproof boots, as the floors are wet almost everywhere.

OK, let me tell you about the different areas of the centre. As you come in through the main entrance, you're in the Discovery Hall. Volunteers there mainly answer visitors' questions about the exhibits.
To the left is the Rock Pool Room. Here, children can touch starfish and crabs, so if you work there, your job is to supervise them and make sure the animals are handled gently.
Beyond that is the Seal Hospital. Only qualified vets treat the animals, but volunteers prepare their food, mostly fish, every morning.
Upstairs you'll find the Research Lab. Volunteers there help our scientists by entering data from our beach surveys into the computer system.

Outside, next to the harbour wall, is the Turtle Pool. This is where turtles recover before release, and volunteers check the water temperature three times a day, as turtles are very sensitive to cold.
Finally, there's the Gift Shop by the exit. Paid staff do all the selling there, but volunteers stand by the door and collect donations from visitors as they leave.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Leila and Sam, discuss their presentation on urban heat islands.
script: Hi, Leila. Shall we go over the presentation on urban heat islands? It's only a week until the seminar.
Yes, good idea. I've read the feedback Dr Evans gave on our outline.
Mostly positive, but she thinks we're trying to cover too much. She said she'd rather we explained a few causes really clearly than listed every possible one.
Fair enough. I was worried about the time limit anyway. Did she mention the sources?
She said they were fine. Actually, she liked that we used the satellite data.

The thing I found most surprising in my reading was how big the temperature difference can be. I'd assumed it was one or two degrees, but some cities are up to ten degrees hotter at night than the countryside around them.
Yes, and it's the night-time difference that's biggest, because concrete releases the heat it stored during the day.
For our own data, I think the survey went really well. We got over two hundred responses.
True, though I'm not sure how reliable it is. Most of the people who answered were students like us, so it's hardly representative of the whole city.
That's a good point. We should mention that as a limitation.
How shall we divide the speaking?
Well, you're more confident with the graphs, so why don't you explain the data, and I'll do the background and the solutions?
Fine by me. And for the ending, I thought we might show a short video.
Hmm, the projector in that room has been unreliable. I'd rather we finished with a question for the audience, to get a discussion going.
Let's go through each section. The introduction, I think, works well as it is.
Then the history of the idea, from the first studies in London in the 1800s.
It's interesting, but it takes nearly four minutes. Could we cut it down to one?
Then the case study of Dhaka. People won't be able to picture it from text alone.
Let's include some photos, maybe the before and after pictures of the green roofs project.
What about the section on air conditioning? It's a bit off topic.
You're right. Let's take it out completely.
And the cost of the solutions, like tree planting. I'm not sure the figures I found are accurate.
Let's check with Dr Evans before we decide.
And the survey results? I was wondering whether to put them at the end instead.
No, they lead naturally into the solutions. Let's keep them where they are.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on communication between plants.
script: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is on a topic that would have sounded like science fiction thirty years ago: the idea that plants can communicate.

Let's start with the history. In 1983, two researchers reported that willow trees attacked by caterpillars appeared to warn nearby, undamaged trees. Those neighbours then produced chemicals that made their leaves harder for insects to digest. The finding was dismissed by many scientists at the time, mainly because the studies used such small samples that the results could have been due to chance.

Since then, however, the evidence has grown considerably. We now know that when leaves are damaged, they release gases into the air. Neighbouring plants detect these gases and prepare their defences. In tomato plants, for instance, the neighbours begin producing compounds that make their leaves taste bitter, so insects are less likely to eat them.

Communication also seems to happen underground. The roots of most plants are connected to vast networks of fungi. The fungi supply the plant with minerals, and in return they receive sugar. Because these networks link many plants together, the forest ecologist Suzanne Simard and her colleagues described them as the wood wide web. Simard's research suggested that large, old trees, which she called mother trees, pass sugar through the network to young seedlings growing in deep shade, where they cannot produce enough food themselves.

More recently, researchers have looked at sound. A team in Israel found that tomato and tobacco plants under water stress produce ultrasonic clicks. They're far too high for humans to hear, but they can be detected by microphones.

Now, not everyone is comfortable with the word communication. Critics point out that it suggests intention, and plants, which have no brain, cannot intend anything. They prefer to say that plants release signals and that other organisms simply eavesdrop. It's a fair point, and you'll need to be careful with your language in your essays.

Finally, what are the practical applications? In farming, growers could plant what are called companion crops, plants that release warning signals and prepare the main crop to defend itself, which would reduce the need for pesticides. And engineers are developing sensors that could pick up these signals, warning farmers of disease before any symptoms are visible on the leaves.
Next week, we'll move on to an even more controversial question: whether plants have memory.

passages.title: The Return of the Sea Otter
paragraphs: Sea otters are among the smallest marine mammals, yet few animals have had a larger influence on the ecosystems in which they live. Found along the coasts of the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan to California, they spend almost their entire lives in the water, and unlike seals and whales, they have no layer of fat to keep them warm. Instead, they rely on the densest fur of any animal, with up to 150,000 hairs per square centimetre, and on an extraordinarily high metabolism. To fuel it, an adult otter must eat around a quarter of its body weight every day.

That remarkable fur almost led to the species' extinction. From the mid-eighteenth century, hunters from Russia, Britain and the United States killed sea otters in enormous numbers to supply the fur trade, which was particularly profitable in China. By 1911, when an international treaty finally banned commercial hunting, the global population had fallen from an estimated 150,000–300,000 to perhaps 2,000 animals, scattered in a handful of isolated colonies.

The disappearance of the otters had consequences that scientists did not fully understand until the 1970s. Sea otters feed heavily on sea urchins, spiny creatures that graze on kelp, the giant seaweed that forms underwater forests along rocky coasts. Without otters to control them, urchin numbers exploded, and in many places the kelp forests were eaten down to bare rock, creating what researchers call 'urchin barrens'. Because kelp forests provide food and shelter for hundreds of other species, including commercially important fish, their loss affected entire coastal ecosystems.

The American ecologist James Estes demonstrated this connection by comparing Aleutian islands where otters had survived with islands where they had not. Around islands with otters, kelp was abundant; around islands without them, it had almost vanished. Estes's work became one of the best-known examples of a 'keystone species': an animal whose impact on its environment is far greater than its numbers would suggest.

Since the hunting ban, sea otters have made a partial recovery. Some populations, such as those in Alaska, grew rapidly with the help of programmes that moved otters to coasts where they had disappeared. Others have been slower. The California population, which descends from a group of about 50 animals discovered in 1938, still numbers only around 3,000, and its growth has been limited by shark attacks and disease.

The otters' return has not been welcomed by everyone. In parts of Alaska and Canada, fishing communities who harvest shellfish such as crabs and clams complain that otters compete with them for the same resources. However, studies in British Columbia suggest that the overall economic effect of otters may be positive: the recovery of kelp forests increases fish stocks and attracts wildlife tourists, and researchers estimate that these gains outweigh the losses to shellfish fisheries by a considerable margin.

There is also growing interest in the role otters might play in tackling climate change. Kelp grows extremely quickly and absorbs carbon dioxide as it does so. One study estimated that, by protecting kelp forests, otters along the coast from Washington State to Alaska help to store several million additional tonnes of carbon. Although some scientists question these figures, the idea that a small, playful mammal could make a measurable difference to the planet's carbon balance has helped to make the sea otter a symbol of what conservation can achieve.

passages.title: Slow Travel
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the measure of a good holiday was how much could be packed into it. Package tours promised 'seven countries in ten days', and the arrival of budget airlines in the 1990s made it possible to fly to another country for a weekend for less than the price of a train ticket. Yet over the past two decades a counter-movement has emerged. Its supporters call it 'slow travel', and they argue that the best way to experience a place is to stay longer, move less and travel overland whenever possible.

The term borrows from the 'slow food' movement, founded in Italy in 1986 as a protest against the opening of a fast-food restaurant near Rome's Spanish Steps. Slow food promoted local ingredients, traditional cooking and long, shared meals. Slow travel applies similar values to tourism: rather than ticking off famous sights, the slow traveller might rent an apartment in a single village for a month, shop at the local market and learn enough of the language to hold a conversation.

Environmental concerns have given the movement new energy. Aviation accounts for roughly 2.5 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, but for a frequent flyer it is often the largest part of their personal carbon footprint. A return flight from London to New York produces about as much carbon per passenger as a year of heating a typical European home. Travelling by train within Europe, by contrast, can reduce emissions for the same journey by up to 90 percent. In Sweden, the word 'flygskam', meaning 'flight shame', became widely used in 2018, and domestic air passenger numbers fell in the following year.

Supporters also claim that slow travel benefits the places being visited. Mass tourism tends to concentrate visitors in a few famous locations, where they spend relatively little money outside large international hotels. Overcrowding in cities such as Venice and Barcelona has led to protests by residents who feel their neighbourhoods have become theme parks. Slow travellers, who stay longer and spread their spending across small local businesses, are said to leave more money in the community and to place less pressure on its infrastructure.

Then there are the psychological benefits. Research on holiday satisfaction suggests that the pleasure people feel from a trip depends less on how many places they visit than on the quality of their experiences. A study by Dutch researchers in 2010 found that holidaymakers were happier than non-holidaymakers before their trips, because of anticipation, but that for most of them the effect disappeared within weeks of returning home. Only those who reported a 'very relaxed' holiday showed any lasting improvement, and rushing from place to place, the authors noted, is rarely relaxing.

Critics, however, argue that slow travel is a luxury few can afford. A month in a Tuscan village requires not only money but time, and most workers have only a few weeks of paid holiday a year. Long-distance train journeys are frequently more expensive than flights, and for travellers outside Europe, where rail networks are less developed, overland alternatives may simply not exist. Some also point out that the image of the slow traveller, sipping coffee in a quiet square, can itself become a marketing tool, used to sell expensive 'authentic' experiences.

The rise of remote work may change this picture. Since 2020, millions of office workers have discovered that they can do their jobs from anywhere with a reliable internet connection, and several countries, including Portugal, Estonia and Costa Rica, now offer special visas for 'digital nomads'. For these workers, staying in one place for weeks or months is not a luxury but a practical necessity. Whether this will reduce the environmental impact of tourism, or simply create new pressures on popular destinations, remains to be seen.

passages.title: Can Machines Understand Language?
paragraphs: In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing proposed a simple test for machine intelligence. If a person exchanging typed messages with a hidden partner could not reliably tell whether that partner was a human or a computer, Turing argued, then the computer should be considered to be thinking. For decades the test seemed safely out of reach. Early programs such as ELIZA, written in 1966, could imitate a psychotherapist by turning a user's statements into questions, but they collapsed as soon as a conversation moved beyond a few predictable patterns.

Today the situation is very different. Large language models, trained on vast quantities of text from the internet, books and other sources, can write essays, summarise reports, translate between dozens of languages and hold conversations that many users find indistinguishable from those with a person. Some have passed professional examinations in law and medicine. To many observers, it appears that Turing's test has finally been passed. The more interesting question, however, is whether passing it tells us what Turing thought it would.

The basic principle behind these systems is surprisingly simple. A language model is trained to predict the next word, or more precisely the next fragment of a word, in a sequence. By adjusting billions of internal parameters to make better predictions across trillions of examples, the model gradually encodes an enormous amount of information about grammar, facts, styles of writing and even patterns of reasoning. Nobody programs these abilities directly; they emerge from the training process, which is one reason why even the engineers who build such systems cannot fully explain how they arrive at a particular answer.

Sceptics argue that this is precisely why we should not speak of understanding. In an influential 2021 paper, the linguist Emily Bender and her co-authors described language models as 'stochastic parrots': systems that stitch together sequences of words according to probabilities, without any connection to the meaning behind them. A model, they pointed out, has never seen the ocean or tasted salt; it knows only how the words 'ocean' and 'salt' tend to appear alongside other words. On this view, the fluency of its output is a kind of illusion, and the danger is that humans, who naturally attribute minds to anything that speaks, will trust it more than they should.

Others find this argument too simple. They note that to predict text accurately across so many subjects, a model may need to build internal representations of the world that work, in effect, like a simplified map. Researchers have found, for example, that a model trained only on lists of moves from a board game developed an internal picture of the board itself, even though it was never shown one. If something similar happens with language, the line between 'merely predicting' and 'understanding' may be less clear than the parrot metaphor suggests. After all, humans also learn much of what they know about the world, about distant countries, historical events or scientific theories, through words rather than direct experience.

My own view is that the debate is often framed in the wrong terms. Asking whether a machine 'really' understands assumes that understanding is a single thing that a system either has or lacks. Human understanding itself comes in degrees: a child who can recite a poem understands it differently from a literary scholar, and neither understands it exactly as its author did. It may be more useful to ask what particular kinds of understanding a system shows, in which situations, and how reliably. Current models are impressive at some tasks and strikingly weak at others; they can explain a complex scientific idea and then fail a simple puzzle that a ten-year-old would solve.

This more modest approach has practical consequences. For languages with relatively few speakers online, such as many indigenous languages of South America or regional languages of South Asia, there is far less text available, and models perform noticeably worse. A system that seems to 'understand' English may misinterpret a question in Bangla or Swahili in ways that are hard for users to detect. Evaluating models language by language and task by task, rather than declaring that machines either do or do not understand, is the only way to know where they can safely be used.

Turing himself might have appreciated this conclusion. In his 1950 paper he described the question 'Can machines think?' as too meaningless to deserve discussion, and replaced it with a test that could actually be carried out. More than seventy years later, the challenge for researchers is to design new tests that are as practical as his, but that measure what we actually care about.

task1.text: The graph below shows the percentage of households with rooftop solar panels in four countries between 2010 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph compares the proportion of households with rooftop solar panels in Australia, Germany, India and Bangladesh between 2010 and 2025.

Overall, solar panel use rose in all four countries, but Australia saw by far the most dramatic growth and had the highest figure by the end of the period. India, despite starting from the lowest point, recorded the fastest growth in the final five years.

In 2010, Germany led with 8% of households, followed by Australia at 5%, while the figures for Bangladesh and India were negligible, at 1% and 0.5% respectively. Australia then overtook Germany: its share tripled to 15% by 2015 and doubled again to 30% in 2020, before reaching 38% in 2025.

Germany's growth was much steadier, climbing gradually to 20% by 2025. Bangladesh rose to 7% in 2020 and then increased only slightly, to 9%. By contrast, India's adoption accelerated noticeably after 2015, more than doubling from 6% to 14% in the last five years, which meant that it overtook Bangladesh.

task2.text: Some people think that international tourism has brought enormous benefits to many places. Others believe that its disadvantages are greater than its advantages. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: International tourism is now one of the largest industries in the world, and its effects on destinations are hotly debated. While some argue that it has transformed many places for the better, others contend that the damage it causes outweighs the gains. In my view, tourism is beneficial overall, but only where it is carefully managed.

Those who welcome tourism point first to its economic impact. In many developing countries, visitors bring foreign currency and create jobs not only in hotels and restaurants but also for farmers, drivers and craftspeople. Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh, for instance, supports thousands of small businesses that depend almost entirely on visitors. Tourism can also encourage governments to protect natural and cultural sites, since a well-preserved coral reef or historic temple attracts more income than a damaged one.

On the other hand, critics highlight serious costs. Large numbers of visitors can overwhelm fragile environments: beaches become polluted with plastic, and reefs are damaged by boats and careless divers. In popular cities such as Venice, rising rents driven by short-term holiday lets have pushed local residents out of their own neighbourhoods. Moreover, much of the profit often goes to international hotel chains rather than to the local community.

In my opinion, these problems are real, but they are reasons to manage tourism rather than to reject it. Measures such as limiting daily visitor numbers at sensitive sites, charging entry fees that fund conservation, and encouraging locally owned accommodation can reduce the harm while preserving the benefits.

In conclusion, although international tourism can damage environments and communities, I believe its economic and cultural advantages are greater, provided that governments plan carefully for its impact.

speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about Saint Martin's Island, a small coral island off the southern tip of Bangladesh, which I visited with a group of friends during my second year at university. We took a bus overnight to Teknaf and then a ferry across the Bay of Bengal, which took about three hours. To be honest, the journey was exhausting, but the moment the island came into view, with its coconut palms and clear turquoise water, it was completely worth it. We spent two days there. During the day we cycled around the island, which you can do in a couple of hours, and in the evening we sat on the beach and watched the sunset. The highlight for me was snorkelling near the rocks, because I'd never seen live coral before. What made the trip so special, I think, was the sense of being completely disconnected. There was hardly any phone signal, so we actually talked to each other instead of staring at our screens. It also made me realise how fragile places like that are, because there was quite a lot of plastic on some beaches. So it was both a relaxing trip and a bit of an eye-opener.
